title: A new commandment (John 13:31–38)
hook: love one another as I have loved you; by this all will know

segments.voice: Yesterday, the beloved disciple leaned on Jesus's chest, and Judas took the bread and went out. Your line was and it was night. Who did you lean on? Day six hundred thirty.

Ever wonder why the Thursday before Easter is called Maundy Thursday? Maundy is an odd word. Outside this one week, English hardly uses it. It comes from Latin. In the old Latin Bible, today's verse begins with the words mandatum novum, a new commandment. Mandatum became maundy. So a whole day of the Christian year is named after one sentence Jesus spoke at supper, right after Judas walked out into the night. The door has just closed behind him. The room is quieter now. And Jesus speaks to the eleven who are left, like a father at the end.

He calls them little children, the only time in John's Gospel he does, and tells them he's going where they can't follow yet. Then: "A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another." Love one another isn't new on its own. The law of Moses already says, love thy neighbor as thyself. Jesus himself quoted it. So what's new? The measure. As I have loved you. Not as you love yourself, but as he has loved them, and they've just seen what that looks like: a towel, a basin, and feet, including the feet of the one who left. Then the sign: "By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another." Not by a badge, a building, or a set of correct opinions. By love they can see. Around the year two hundred, a Christian writer in North Africa named Tertullian reported what outsiders said about the Christians they knew: see how they love one another. Then Peter interrupts. Lord, where are you going? Why can't I follow you now? "I will lay down my life for thy sake." He means it. And Jesus answers with sad honesty: "The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice." Even the friend who promises the most will fail tonight. The new commandment is given to people who will need it. Look back over this week: a frightened council, nard filling a house, a grain of wheat, walking in the light, a towel and basin, a disciple leaning close, and now love as the sign.
screen: `PETER: I WILL LAY DOWN MY LIFE.`
then, large: `AS I HAVE LOVED YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: love someone visibly. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone in your life whose love for you has been visible. Not just felt, but seen. Something they did. Remember it clearly. Now think of someone you love, but maybe not visibly enough. A friend, a family member, someone in your community. What could you do today that they would actually see? Not a big gesture. A note, a meal, an hour, showing up. Picture it. If you pray, you can ask to love as you've been loved. If you don't, simply decide on the one thing. The bell holds the time.
Tertullian. A Christian writer in North Africa who reported what outsiders said of believers: see how they love one another.
Your line: by this, all will know. Today, do the one visible act of love you chose, where it can be seen by the person it's for. Day six hundred thirty, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: Christians remember the new commandment on Maundy Thursday, often with footwashing, communion and the stripping of the altar; many churches also take it as the measure of their common life.

original.note: Greek: new, fresh. A new commandment: the old command to love, with a new measure.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus invented the command to love one another.
what it means: the command to love is old; what's new is the measure, as I have loved you, shown with a towel and a basin.
what a scholar hears: the Latin mandatum novum gave English Maundy Thursday, and Tertullian reports outsiders saying, see how they love one another.

sources.quoted: A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another.
By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.
I will lay down my life for thy sake.
The cock shall not crow, till thou hast denied me thrice.

notes: 'Little children' (teknia, 13:33): the only time in John's Gospel Jesus uses this word (1 John uses it often). Confirm.
'Love thy neighbor as thyself' is close to KJV Leviticus 19:18 ('thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself'); paraphrased with American spelling, not marked as quotation. Confirm.
Etymology Maundy < Latin mandatum (Vulgate John 13:34, 'Mandatum novum do vobis'): standard. Confirm.
Tertullian, Apology 39 (c. AD 197): 'see how they love one another' paraphrased. Confirm.

Audit (y2 10% sample): 'nobody uses it anywhere else' was untrue (e.g. Britain's Royal Maundy, itself a Maundy Thursday custom); softened. 'The one who loves him most' was an unsourced ranking of the disciples; changed to 'the friend who promises the most'.
